segments.text: Welcome to your daily Robotics digest for November 17th, 2026.
We've got deep dives on self-improving agents, the need for physical AI, and massive humanoid robot rollouts.
Tune in for the news.

From thesequence.substack.com, The Sequence Knowledge - Issue number nine hundred seventy-three discusses learning reinforcement learning from interacting with world models as training grounds for self-improving agents.

DeepMind's work explores using learned simulators to generate the consequences of actions, creating experience on demand which, when integrated with task proposal and evaluation systems, forms an improvement machinery.
Early examples of this setup are demonstrated through systems such as SIMA two and Genie three.

The discussion examines whether this generated experience imparts transferable capabilities and analyzes the economic cost associated with experience generation and the recursive nature of improvement.
This research indicates a pathway for creating agents capable of self-directed skill enhancement through simulated interaction.
Future developments will focus on assessing the quality and generality of these self-generated skills.
From Robotics & Automation News, "Opinion: Moravec’s paradox explains why physical AI needs a sense of touch."
This story examines how Moravec's paradox illustrates the difficulty in achieving physical artificial intelligence due to the gap between intellectual ease and physical interaction.
The disconnect stems from the fact that human sensory processing evolved to conceal complex physical computations below conscious awareness, creating a major hurdle for physical AI systems.
The physical point of contact proves challenging because visual systems lack the necessary data to process real-world resistance.
Integrating force and torque sensing into robotic systems allows them to perceive the physical world directly rather than relying only on visual predictions.
Grounding physical AI necessitates incorporating precise, real-time sensory feedback into the fundamental hardware architecture.
This shift indicates a direction for advancing physical robotics development.
From Robotics & Automation News, GXO and Apptronik plan a rollout of up to one thousand humanoid robots.
This story details a partnership for a Robotics-as-a-Service model to deploy humanoid robots in logistics operations.
The collaboration focuses on applying these robots to tasks such as goods-to-person picking, case movement, and sortation within warehouse workflows.
Joint trials involving the Apollo robot in live operations will commence in 2027 to validate safety and performance against agreed key performance indicators.
If these trials are successful, the companies intend to implement a global rollout of up to one thousand humanoid robots over four years, beginning in North America in late 2027.
This initiative seeks to utilize physical artificial intelligence to enhance logistics by enabling humanoids to work alongside existing automation and personnel.
The success of this phased deployment will set a benchmark for physical AI integration in supply chain management.
From Humanoid.guide, "Booster T2 targets developers with an open humanoid platform".
This report details how Booster Robotics is offering its T2 humanoid as an open platform for the development of robot intelligence through accessible APIs and software development kits.
The company supplies the necessary hardware and operating system tools while focusing investment on advancing AI models and algorithms.
The T2 robot measures one point four meters in height and weighs forty-two kilograms, featuring thirty-one degrees of freedom and interchangeable end effectors.

The platform incorporates tools such as Booster Studio for simulation and deployment, granting developers control over model behavior, with operational safety and integration depending on the customer-supplied software stack and task complexity.
This development indicates a push toward democratizing access to humanoid robotics development.
The industry should observe further advancements in accessible robotic platforms.
From The Robot Report, "The hidden reason most robots fail on the factory floor".
This segment examines the primary cause of robot failure on the factory floor, which is attributed to a lack of real-world application.
Standard Bots co-founder Evan Beard details that the failure stems from the robots not being adequately tested in practical industrial settings.
Standard Bots designs and assembles its robotics systems internally, managing the entire stack from hardware to artificial intelligence.

Beard further suggests a coordinated United States robotics strategy is necessary for industry advancement, noting that Intel is contributing to this progress by providing a platform that integrates artificial intelligence inference, sensing, and real-time control for robotics.
The future direction for robotics is centered on ensuring these machines achieve functionality within actual operational environments.
This focus indicates that practical deployment remains the critical barrier for advancing the artificial intelligence and technology sectors.
From IEEE Spectrum - Robotics, "Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?".
This story details the development of a robotic system intended to facilitate remote stroke surgery, specifically thrombectomies.
Remedy Robotics is developing the N1 system, which utilizes a robotic arm and steerable catheter controlled remotely to extend specialized care to remote and rural areas.
The technology aims to overcome geographic barriers for patients requiring time-critical stroke treatment by employing remote operation techniques.
Successful telesurgery implementation is contingent upon establishing robust communication infrastructure and optimizing latency while maintaining patient safety protocols.
Researchers are actively focusing on improving the speed and safety of these remote procedures to expand access to emergency stroke care.
This advancement signals a potential shift in the deployment of advanced robotics within critical medical infrastructure.

From Robotics & Automation News, Richtech Robotics to unveil an AI-powered cleaning system at the ISSA Show 2026, detailing a system that connects autonomous cleaning robots, camera monitoring, and operational data for intelligent and responsive hygiene management.
Richtech Robotics will present its Intelligent Cleaning System at the ISSA Show North America 2026 in Las Vegas.
The system integrates existing indoor CCTV with Dust-E robots to automatically identify and execute targeted cleaning tasks.
A centralized dashboard provides facility intelligence, tracking robot locations, records, and alerts for maintenance.
This system utilizes the integration of autonomous robots with visual data to manage hygiene operations efficiently.
Richtech Robotics will also showcase various robots and present on building complete robotics floor care programs.
The unveiling signifies advancements in applied artificial intelligence for sophisticated industrial and commercial maintenance solutions.
From Humanoid.guide, "Hyundai takes full Boston Dynamics ownership for Atlas push".
This report details the acquisition of Boston Dynamics by Hyundai Motor Group affiliates, leading to full ownership of the Atlas humanoid robots.

The transaction facilitates Hyundai's objective to establish an annual production capacity of thirty thousand Atlas humanoids by two thousand twenty-eight, with initial deployment scheduled at a Georgia facility.
The acquisition involved Hyundai Glovis investing forty-six point five billion won and Hyundai Motor separately.

These Atlas robots are slated for initial use in sorting and transporting automotive parts at the Hyundai Motor Group Metaplant America in Georgia, and the full ownership streamlines funding and deployment coordination for Atlas development.
This move signals a significant step toward scaling humanoid robotics within the automotive technology sector.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, Pelican VL 2.0!".
This segment reports on the introduction of Pelican VL 2.0, an embodied AI foundation model developed by the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center.
The model functions as the brain layer of a robotics system, operating separately from the physical body or motor controller.
The Brain Score for this model is reported at two out of ten, indicating an early stage of autonomy that necessitates a measured evaluation approach.
This model is being offered as a commercial service, extending beyond the center's existing Tiangong ecosystem.
A key distinction in this development is the separation of the foundation model from the motion controller to facilitate proper system assessment.
This development signals an advancement in modular robotics architecture and the commercialization of embodied AI components.
Industry focus should remain on the independent evaluation of such foundation models.
From Humanoid.guide, "Welcome, AstraBrain!".

This report details the architecture and performance of the AstraBrain system, which functions as an embodied AI software system for humanoid robots developed by Beijing Galbot AI Co., Ltd., achieving a Humanoid.Guide Brain Score of eight out of ten.
The system's architecture incorporates a planning component designated as the brain, a body control component referred to as the cerebellum, and a connecting bridge module.
The controller for this system is named AstraBrain WBC, emphasizing the distinct separation between the planning and control layers within the design.
This software layer serves as a shared interface across Galbot's range of robotics.
The system was presented at the World Robot Conference in August 2026.
This development indicates advancements in the modular design of embodied AI systems for robotics.
Further developments in this area warrant observation from the technology sector.
From Robotics & Automation News, Penguin Random House doubles book picking productivity with Locus Robotics.
This report details how the company modernized its book distribution in its Barcelona operation using Locus Robotics, resulting in a significant increase in picking efficiency.
Penguin Random House Grupo Editorial implemented Locus Robotics to manage fragmented and seasonal demand within its Barcelona facility.
The deployment scaled from fourteen robots to forty, managing nearly one thousand stock keeping units, and the system now handles over one and a half million units monthly.

This automation increased picking productivity to over five hundred and ten units per hour compared to manual methods, and the flexible infrastructure allowed for scaling through demand variability without operational disruption during facility transitions.
This development demonstrates the increasing applicability of advanced robotics in complex logistics environments.
From Robohub, "Robot swarms trained by trial and error in simulation keep working on real robots".
This report details a method used by researchers to ensure the reliable performance of robot swarms when transitioning from simulation to physical hardware.
The research involved training reinforcement learning agents in simulation and then deploying these learned skills onto physical robots, addressing the challenge known as the reality gap.
To mitigate simulation inaccuracies, the learning algorithm was restricted to selecting from a set of previously tested behaviors instead of directly controlling every motor.
Experiments conducted with twenty e-puck robots demonstrated that this approach significantly outperformed other methodologies in achieving complex real-world tasks.
This work establishes a pathway for reliable swarm robotics by bridging the gap between simulation-based learning and physical execution.
The development suggests a more robust approach for deploying artificial intelligence in complex robotic systems.
From The Robot Report, Agile Robots raises five hundred million dollars to increase production capacity.
This report details the recent Series F funding secured by the company, resulting in a valuation of eight point five billion dollars and a total funding amount of two billion dollars.
Agile Robots develops and deploys a range of robotic systems including humanoids mobile robots and robotic arms coupled with their software and artificial intelligence models.
The raised capital will be allocated to expanding production capacity and broadening the company's market presence in significant global regions.

The company intends to integrate physical artificial intelligence into industrial production across sectors such as automotive and manufacturing, currently expanding its manufacturing capabilities with the addition of a facility in Germany to address escalating demand.
This expansion indicates a continued push for the integration of advanced physical AI into widespread industrial applications.
And that's all for today's robotic roundup!
Diving into world models is the next big leap.
Thanks for tuning in to the future of robotics.
Until tomorrow, keep building smart things!
